title: Store and app install details in the Dev Dashboard
summary:
You can now view your organization’s installed apps, collaborator access, earnings, and app activity in one place in the Dev Dashboard.

Use the store page to view apps, users, and earnings for a store:

  • Apps from your organization installed on the store.
  • Users in your organization who have collaborator access to the store.
  • Earnings from the store, including total app earnings, total theme earnings, and recurring revenue share.

You can also dig in by app, with app install details:

  • Gross lifetime earnings from that store for the selected app.
  • An activity feed of installation and billing events.
  • The app’s current subscription, with quick access to logs for that store.

To get started, select a store in Stores in the Dev Dashboard. For app install details, open your app’s Overview, select the install count in the Installs card, then select a store. Available details depend on your permissions and store access.

Learn more about store details and app install details, including available information and permissions.

title: Manage payouts, billing, and settings in Dev Dashboard
summary:
You now manage your Partner business details, payouts, billing, and the remaining Partner Dashboard settings in Dev Dashboard's Organization settings. New Partners also complete business verification there during setup. Existing Partners don’t need to take action because your current payout and billing settings stay the same.

What changed

The Settings and Payouts links in Partner Dashboard and the Home payout widget have moved to Dev Dashboard. To reach the new pages, open Dev Dashboard, select your organization, and open Organization settings.

From Organization settings, you can manage:

  • Organization details: business and contact details, emergency contact, App Store registration, and Partner ID
  • Payouts: payout setup, history, transactions, and payout methods
  • Partner billing: bills, ad invoices, payment methods, invoice notes, and ad credits
  • Users > Security: Partner API clients

What to do

Your payout or billing settings are migrated over, and no action is required.

To learn more about where Partner Dashboard features have moved in Dev Dashboard, see the migration guide. For more about Dev Dashboard in general, see the Overview.

title: Security update: Offline token dates, new security features
summary:
On October 20, we asked all app devs to secure their app, and told you we'd share more before any security change takes effect. Here's what's new, and what you need to do.

Offline access tokens

The migration timeline for offline access tokens remains the same: All public apps that call the Admin API must migrate to expiring offline access tokens by January 1, 2027. We're sharing an updated enforcement timeline if an app isn't migrated by then:

  • January 1, 2027: Delisted from the Shopify App Store and blocked from new installs. Existing installs keep working.
  • January 15, 2027: Merchants using the app see a warning in Shopify admin.
  • April 1, 2027: Admin API requests using non-expiring offline access tokens return HTTP 403.

January 1 is the migration deadline: The later dates give merchants time to prepare, and should not be treated as extra time to migrate. Custom apps, merchant-created apps and online access tokens are not affected. Follow the migration guide.

New security features

We've rolled out several new features this week to help secure your app:

  • Recover access with client credentials. If your app loses a refresh token, your backend can now request a new access token signed with your app's private key, without waiting for a merchant to reopen your app. Set up client credentials access.
  • Restrict API access to your own servers with an IP allowlist. List the IP addresses your servers use, and we'll reject Admin API requests from any other IP, even if it has a valid access token. Set up your IP allowlist.
  • Tell us which servers and sites your app uses. In the new [network_access] section of shopify.app.toml, list the servers your app's code loads from or sends requests to, wherever it runs on a store. We use that list to spot requests your app didn't make. You can also list the sites you link customers to, so those links skip the warning customers normally see before leaving the store. Declare your app's network access.
  • We now verify your identity before installing apps on development and client-transfer stores. This helps keep apps in trusted hands.
  • Use the new app security hub as your checklist. Every app security practice now has its own page in the dev docs. Point your agent at the hub to check which practices apply to your app, and run shopify app security check before every release. Go to the app security hub.

Get help

If you ever suspect a security issue with your app, notify us immediately at partner-security-reports@shopify.com. You are accountable to fix the problem and notify affected merchants, and we'll support you through it.

For general security inquiries, contact Shopify Support.

Questions about these updates? Ask in the App Security board in the developer community.

title: Migrate to expiring offline access tokens before January 1, 2027
summary:
Public apps still using non-expiring offline access tokens must migrate to use expiring offline access tokens before January 1, 2027 to remain listed in the Shopify App Store and continue accepting new installs.

New client credentials access helps your backend recover access without waiting for a merchant to reopen your app. Using a request signed with your app's private key, your backend can obtain a fresh, short-lived access token without a refresh token.

The enforcement timeline has been updated with incremental penalties for non-compliant apps:

  • January 1, 2027: Non-compliant apps are delisted from the Shopify App Store and blocked from new installs. Existing installations can continue making affected API requests until April 1.
  • January 15, 2027: Merchants using non-compliant apps see warnings in Shopify admin about the risk of service interruption and the action they can take.
  • April 1, 2027: Affected Admin API requests using non-expiring offline access tokens return HTTP 403.

This schedule applies to existing public apps previously covered by the January 1, 2027 deadline. The requirement for public apps created on or after April 1, 2026 remains in effect. Custom apps and apps created by merchants are excluded.

Follow the migration guide to update token acquisition, migrate existing installations, and validate token storage and refresh handling.

title: Secure your app with network access rules in `shopify.app.toml`
summary:
You can now declare your app's external hosts and servers in a new [network_access] section of shopify.app.toml. Normally Shopify warns customers when they navigate to a URL ouside Shopify; declaring your external hosts skips this warning, letting you remove friction for trusted journeys. Declaring servers, meanwhile, helps Shopify spot suspicious activity and protect your app.

What changed

The new network_access section has two properties:

  • allowed_navigation_hosts: The external sites your app links to from the storefront, such as your own domain. Shopify normally warns customers before sending them to a site outside the storefront. Links to these hosts skip that warning. List each host exactly as it appears in your links, up to 20.
  • allowed_sources: Up to 20 HTTPS origins that your app's code loads from or sends requests to on storefront, checkout, and Shopify admin pages. This includes your extensions, app home, and app proxy pages. We use the list to protect your app and monitor storefronts for malicious requests.

Here's an example configuration:

[network_access]
allowed_navigation_hosts = ["app.example.com"]
allowed_sources = ["https://api.app.example.com"]

Who's affected

Any app whose code links to or contacts external servers from a storefront, checkout, or the Shopify admin can use the new section.

What to do

For all apps, we strongly recommend you:

  1. Add the hosts that your app links customers to, such as your app's own site, to allowed_navigation_hosts.
  2. Add the servers that your app's code loads from or sends requests to, such as your API or CDN, to allowed_sources.
  3. Run shopify app deploy and release the new version.

For examples, see Declare your app's network access.

title: Restrict Admin API access with an IP allowlist
summary:
You can now limit Admin API access tokens by IP address. When you add your servers' IP addresses to an IP allowlist in the Dev Dashboard, Shopify rejects GraphQL Admin API and REST Admin API requests that use your app's tokens from anywhere else.

What changed

Your app's Settings page has a new IP allowlist section. Enter your servers' addresses or CIDR ranges, test them against recent traffic, and enable enforcement. Requests from outside your ranges fail with a 403 status code.

What to do

We strongly recommend using an IP allowlist if your app calls Shopify from static IP addresses. For setup instructions, see Restrict API access with an IP allowlist.

Note: Support for apps hosted on serverless platforms with dynamic IP addresses is coming soon.

title: Promoted Placements beta now includes Shop Campaigns
summary:
Promoted Placements is now in beta, and it includes Shop Campaigns. When a search_catalog result comes from a merchant running Shop Campaigns, you earn the commission that merchant funds, added to Shopify's base rate. No action is required.

What changed

Merchants running Shop Campaigns with external platforms turned on now include the Catalog API as one of those platforms. On their products, placement.commission.percentage.value returns the total rate, combining the merchant's commission and Shopify's base rate. Buyers who click a product with merchant-funded commission land in Shop (shop.com).

Who is affected

Organizations in the Promoted Placements beta that have accepted the terms and turned on Earn commission for a saved catalog. Access is invite-led, and you can join the waitlist from the docs.

What to do

No action is required, because commission comes back in the same field you already read. Keep passing your enrolled catalog.catalog_id on search_catalog and send buyers to the variant URL exactly as Shopify returns it. If you show a commission rate in your own reporting, read it from placement.commission.percentage.value, since it now varies by product.

Earning applies to search_catalog only, and only to products from Shopify merchants.

Related docs

  • Catalog API

title: Search brands that don't sell on Shopify in the Catalog API (beta)
summary:
You can now return products from brands that don't sell on Shopify when you search the beta Catalog API. Add the new sources parameter to search_catalog to include external products in the same response as products from Shopify merchants. If you omit sources, results stay limited to Shopify merchant products and you don't need to change any existing calls.

What changed

The Catalog API beta now supports a sources parameter on search_catalog that controls which products you return:

  • Shopify merchant products only: omit sources, or set ["shopify"]
  • Both Shopify merchant and external products: ["shopify", "external"]
  • Brands that don't sell on Shopify only: ["external"]

The sources parameter works on the existing search_catalog method, with no new endpoint to call. The get_product method returns an external product when you pass its ID, and lookup_catalog support is coming later.

External products always return eligible.native_checkout: false, so shoppers can't buy them through Shopify checkout and these products don't earn Promoted Placements commission. Each external product includes a description, an image, a price, and a link to the brand's product page so the shopper completes the purchase on the brand's own site.

Who’s affected

This change affects apps that use the Catalog API to power on-site search or recommendations and want to include products from brands that don't sell on Shopify.

During the beta, external product data comes from each brand's website, and external products only return when the shopper is in the United States. Searches for shoppers in other countries continue to return Shopify merchant products only.

What to do

No action is required if you only want to keep returning products from Shopify merchants. Your existing search_catalog calls work without changes.

If you want to include external products, update your search_catalog requests to set the sources parameter to ["shopify", "external"], or to ["external"] if you only want brands that don't sell on Shopify. If you surface links to product detail pages, make sure you handle external product URLs correctly so shoppers land on the brand’s own site when they select an external product.

Related docs

  • Learn how to return products from brands that don't sell on Shopify in the Catalog API: https://shopify.dev/docs/agents/catalog/global-catalog-extension#catalog-sources
  • Read more about Global Catalog MCP tools: https://shopify.dev/docs/agents/catalog/global-catalog

title: Analytics queryable capability is configurable in shopify.app.toml for metaobject definitions
summary:
Apps can now set capabilities.analytics_queryable on metaobject definitions in shopify.app.toml. This makes compatible fields on those definitions queryable in Shopify analytics and ShopifyQL. It applies to apps that declare metaobject definitions in their app configuration. No action is required, because the capability stays off unless you add the key.

What changed

Metaobject definitions declared under [metaobjects.app.] in shopify.app.toml now accept capabilities.analytics_queryable. When you set it to true, any field on the definition with an analytics-compatible type, such as single_line_text_field, number_integer, date, or product_reference, becomes available as a dimension and filter in analytics reports and ShopifyQL. This works wherever a product, product variant, customer, or order metafield references the metaobject. Fields with other types are ignored.

Previously, an app could only set this capability through the GraphQL Admin API, and only on definitions it didn't manage in TOML. Declarative definitions are read-only through the API, so there was no way to make them queryable.

Who's affected

This applies to apps that declare metaobject definitions in shopify.app.toml. Existing definitions don't change. If a definition doesn't include the key, the capability stays off.

It doesn't apply to these:

  • Metaobject definitions that you create with the GraphQL Admin API. For those, set analyticsQueryable with the metaobjectDefinitionCreate or metaobjectDefinitionUpdate mutation in API version 2027-01 or later.
  • Metaobject definitions that merchants own. Merchants turn analytics on or off for those in the Shopify admin.

What to do

No action is required. To make a declared metaobject definition queryable in analytics:

  1. Add capabilities.analytics_queryable = true to the definition in shopify.app.toml, and make sure at least one of its fields has an analytics-compatible type.
  2. Deploy your app configuration to a development store.
  3. Confirm that the definition's capabilities.analyticsQueryable.enabled field is true in GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01 or later, and that its fields appear in analytics reports for the product, variant, customer, or order metafield that references it.
[metaobjects.app.designer]
name = "Designer"
capabilities.analytics_queryable = true

[metaobjects.app.designer.fields.country]
name = "Country"
type = "single_line_text_field"

This example makes the country field of the designer metaobject queryable. Replace the definition and fields with your own. If none of a definition's fields has a compatible type, the release fails validation, so add or change a field before you deploy.

Related docs

  • Make your metaobjects queryable in analytics
  • Metaobject TOML reference
  • metaobjectDefinitionCreate mutation

title: Unlink a customer's identity provider subject with the GraphQL Admin API
summary:
As of API version 2027-01, you can use the identityProviderSubjectDelete mutation to unlink a customer from a third-party identity provider.

Pass the customer's ID as customerId and the identity provider subject's ID as id. You can get subject IDs from Customer.identityProviderSubjects. Unlinking signs the customer out of all of their existing sessions. The next time they sign in through the identity provider, they're linked again.

The mutation requires the write_customers access scope.

title: Discover a merchant's retail stores with UCP location search and lookup
summary:
Shopify storefronts now support the UCP location capability, dev.ucp.common.location.search and dev.ucp.common.location.lookup, starting with UCP 2026-08-25. When you negotiate these capabilities over the storefront MCP endpoint, your agent can find a merchant's physical stores, narrow them by name, city, or distance, and check which stores carry the items a buyer wants. This is an optional new capability and doesn't require changes if you don't use locations today.

What changed

Storefronts with at least one retail location now list both location capabilities in their discovery profiles at /.well-known/ucp. A retail location is an active, merchant-managed location that the merchant set up to sell in person and enabled as a Physical storefront.

If your agent profile negotiates these capabilities, the storefront MCP endpoint at https://{storedomain}/api/ucp/mcp exposes two tools:

  • search_locations lists the shop's retail locations. An empty location object returns the first page. You can narrow results with a query that matches store names and cities, a distance relation with an explicit center and a max radius in meters, and filters.items.

title: POS UI extensions now support reactive storage access
summary:
The new shopify.storage.current API lets POS UI extension developers respond automatically when stored values change across extension targets on the same POS device. It’s now available in API version 2026-10. No changes are required for existing extensions.

What changed

shopify.storage.current exposes each storage key as a read-only reactive signal. You can read its current value or subscribe to changes made by other targets of the same extension on the same POS device. Writes and removals still use the existing Storage API methods.

For example, a background target can fetch and store a customer’s loyalty points, and a smart grid tile can react to those changes automatically. This keeps the displayed balance up to date without repeated storage reads or custom polling logic.

Stored values load asynchronously, so a signal’s value is initially undefined until its key finishes loading. Make sure you handle this initial state as well as missing keys.

Who’s affected

This addition is available to POS UI extensions that use API version 2026-10 or later. Extensions that use earlier API versions can’t use shopify.storage.current.

What to do

You don’t need to take action. Existing Storage API methods continue to work as before.

To adopt reactive storage, update your extension to use API version 2026-10 or later and read or subscribe to the keys your extension needs through shopify.storage.current.

Related docs

  • POS UI extensions Storage API reference

title: POS UI extensions 2026-10 adds s-pos-list, a virtualized list with custom row templates
summary:
POS UI extensions API version 2026-10 adds s-pos-list, a virtualized list component for Polaris web components. You pass rows as plain data and lay out each kind of row with a template built from web components. s-pos-list is now available in Shopify POS 11.17.0 and later, and it replaces the List component from API version 2025-07 and earlier for extensions that adopt 2026-10. No action is required.

What changed

The List component ended with API version 2025-07, and Polaris web components had no list component to replace it. s-pos-list fills that gap. Instead of List’s fixed row layout, each kind of row gets its own template, so one list can mix headings, dividers, and content rows.

Who's affected

Extensions that set api_version = "2026-10" and run on Shopify POS 11.17.0 or later can use s-pos-list. API version 2026-07 and earlier don’t include it, and nothing changes for extensions that stay on earlier API versions or keep using List.

It’s for extensions that used List and are moving to Polaris web components, and for extensions that build long lists by mapping rows into s-scroll-box.

Why this matters

Mapping rows into s-scroll-box makes POS create a view for every row, so display time and memory grow with the list, and very large lists can fail to display. s-pos-list recycles row views as the POS user scrolls. In testing on an iPad (A16) with the most complex List row layout, s-pos-list displays and scrolls large lists as fast as the 2025-07 List.

What to do

You don’t need to change existing extensions, because s-pos-list is a new component and existing extensions keep working unchanged. When you adopt API version 2026-10 and run on Shopify POS 11.17.0 or later, you can use the following mappings to move List implementations to s-pos-list:

| List (2025-07) | s-pos-list (2026-10) | |

title: Metaobject analytics queryable capability available in the Admin API
summary:
Starting with GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01, you can read and configure the analyticsQueryable capability on metaobject definitions. This applies to apps that create, update, or inspect metaobject definitions. No action is required unless you want your app to control whether a metaobject definition can be queried in analytics.

What changed

The GraphQL Admin API now exposes the analytics queryable capability for metaobject definitions.

You can read MetaobjectCapabilities.analyticsQueryable, which includes:

  • eligible: whether the metaobject definition can use the capability. A definition is eligible if at least one of its fields uses an analytics-compatible type.
  • enabled: whether the capability is currently enabled.

You can also set the capability when you create or update a metaobject definition by using:

  • MetaobjectCapabilityCreateInput.analyticsQueryable
  • MetaobjectCapabilityUpdateInput.analyticsQueryable
  • MetaobjectCapabilityAnalyticsQueryableInput.enabled

The MetaobjectCapabilityType enum now includes ANALYTICS_QUERYABLE, and MetaobjectUserErrorCode includes CAPABILITY_NOT_ELIGIBLE for definitions that can’t enable the capability.

Who's affected

This change applies to apps that use GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01 or later to create, update, or inspect metaobject definitions.

Apps that use earlier versions don’t see the analyticsQueryable field, input, enum value, or error code. Existing apps don’t need to make changes unless they want to support analytics queryability for metaobject definitions.

Why this matters

You can now determine whether a metaobject definition is eligible to be queried in analytics and enable that capability through the public GraphQL Admin API. This brings metaobject definitions in line with metafield definitions, and you get consistent control over which custom data types appear in analytics.

What to do

No action is required.

If you want to use this capability:

  1. Update your app to use GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01 or later.
  2. Update your metaobject definition queries or mutations to include analyticsQueryable.

For example, to read a metaobject definition’s capabilities, include:

capabilities {
  analyticsQueryable {
    eligible
    enabled
  }
}

When you create or update a metaobject definition, set analyticsQueryable.enabled in the capability input. Check eligible first, and handle CAPABILITY_NOT_ELIGIBLE in mutation user errors. Use this method to confirm whether a definition supports the capability and give clear feedback when it doesn't.

Related docs

  • GraphQL Admin API reference
  • Metaobjects in Shopify apps

title: Securing your app, together
summary:
Merchants install your app because they trust it, and because they trust the Shopify App Store. There are bad actors out there who are motivated to exploit that trust. Alongside the rest of the industry, we are seeing the number of attacks increasing across the app ecosystem as AI gets better at finding vulnerabilities.

Security is the most important thing you can work on right now. We’re asking every app developer to act on the steps below this week.

  • Scan your app with our new security check. A single prompt with AI Toolkit checks for Shopify-specific vulnerabilities, such as unauthenticated routes, cross-shop data access and unverified webhooks. In early access, most partners found something they didn’t know about.
  • Move to expiring access tokens. Short-lived tokens limit the damage if a token leaks. This will soon be required for all public apps, so start your migration now.
  • Use vulnerability scanners to ensure all endpoints of your app are secured.
  • Treat all rendered data, whether pulled from metafields or your own servers, as untrusted, ensuring inputs are thoroughly escaped and sanitized.
  • Check your Dev Dashboard to look at your API requests and ensure you do not see any suspicious activity. To get started, filter your logs by client IP to look at traffic patterns and find suspicious sources.
  • Protect every account that touches your app. Turn on two-step authentication for your Partner account, hosting, CDN, code repositories and email. Remove access for anyone who no longer needs it.
  • Keep your emergency contact current. Make sure your emergency developer email in the Partner Dashboard reaches someone who can act quickly.
  • Review and apply the security best practices in Shopify Dev Docs.

What we’re doing alongside you

We’re tightening the boundaries for storefront app code, adding IP address restrictions so your keys only work from your servers, and raising App Store security requirements. We’ll share details and timelines with you before any change takes effect, so you have time to prepare. We’ll keep investing in platform protections, developer tools and guidance that make secure development the default.

If you ever suspect a security issue with your app, notify us immediately at partner-security-reports@shopify.com. You are accountable to fix the problem and notify affected merchants, and we’ll support you through it.

For general security inquiries, contact Shopify Support.

title: Enable the analytics queryable capability on metafield and metaobject definitions from your app's TOML
summary:
You can now enable the analytics_queryable capability on metafield and metaobject definitions that you declare in shopify.app.toml. Merchants can then use those metafields and metaobjects as dimensions and filters in Shopify Analytics and ShopifyQL. Previously, you could set this capability only through the GraphQL Admin API.

What changed

Declarative definitions accept a new capability: capabilities.analytics_queryable. When it's true, the definition's values become queryable in analytics, the same as when you set analyticsQueryable with the metafieldDefinitionCreate ,metafieldDefinitionUpdate, metaobjectDefinitionCreate, and metaobjectDefinitionUpdate mutation. 

[customer.metafields.app.membership_level]
name = "Membership level"
type = "single_line_text_field"
capabilities.analytics_queryable = true

[metaobjects.app.ingredient]
name = "Ingredient"
capabilities.analytics_queryable = true

[metaobjects.app.ingredient.fields.name]
type = "single_line_text_field"
name = "Name"

[metaobjects.app.ingredient.fields.calories]
type = "number_integer"
name = "Calories"

Release your app version with shopify app deploy, and Shopify distributes the definition to every shop where your app is installed.

What you need to know

  • The capability is available for customer, order, product, and product variant metafield definitions.
  • Not every metafield type can be queried in analytics. To confirm that a definition can use the capability, check the eligible field on its analyticsQueryable capability.
  • A metaobject definition can use the capability only if at least one of its fields has an analytics-compatible type.

For more information, refer to the following resources:

  • Use metafield capabilities
  • TOML reference for metafield definitions
  • Metaobject analytics queryable capability available in the Admin API.

title: Exclusive > timestamp filters exclude the full second
summary:
As of API version 2026-10, an exclusive lower bound (>) on a timestamp filter in the GraphQL Admin API search syntax excludes the full second. For example, created_at:>'2026-09-15T12:00:02Z' no longer returns an order created at 12:00:02.500.

What changed

The GraphQL Admin API returns timestamps such as createdAt to the second, but internally some resources store them with fractional seconds.

Before 2026-10, created_at:>'2026-09-15T12:00:02Z' compared against 12:00:02.000000. It returned records from later in that second, and the response showed those records with createdAt: "2026-09-15T12:00:02Z". The same records also matched created_at:<='2026-09-15T12:00:02Z'.

As of 2026-10, when a > value has no fractional seconds, the filter starts after the end of that second (12:00:02.999999). A record matches >T only when the timestamp that the API returns for it is later than T, so >T and <=T no longer overlap.

These filters don't change on any version: >=, <, and <=; date-only values such as created_at:>2026-09-15; and values with fractional seconds such as created_at:>'2026-09-15T12:00:02.250Z'.

Who's affected

Apps that send a > bound without fractional seconds on a timestamp filter in the query argument of a GraphQL Admin API connection, for example created_at on the orders query.

What to do

Apps on 2026-07 or earlier don't need to change anything. Before you move an app to 2026-10, check its > filters:

  1. Find queries that pass a timestamp from an earlier response as a > bound, for example to fetch records newer than the last record that the app saw.
  2. If the app must not miss records created later in that same second, use >= with that timestamp and remove duplicates by id.
query OrdersSinceLastSync {
  orders(first: 50, sortKey: CREATED_AT, query: "created_at:>='2026-09-15T12:00:02Z'") {
    nodes {
      id
      createdAt
    }
  }
}

title: Checkout MCP and Cart MCP now support UCP buyer consent
summary:
Checkout MCP and Cart MCP now support the UCP buyer consent extension (dev.ucp.shopping.buyer_consent) starting with UCP 2026-08-25. Buyers can now make the same privacy and marketing choices in your agent that they'd make in a shop's own checkout, like opting in to email or SMS. Shops receive those choices with the cart, checkout, and order.

What changed

Storefronts now list dev.ucp.shopping.buyer_consent in their discovery profiles at /.well-known/ucp. This extension applies to both cart and checkout.

If your agent profile negotiates dev.ucp.shopping.buyer_consent on UCP 2026-08-25:

  • Checkout MCP and Cart MCP responses include a buyer.consent object.
  • buyer.consent lists each consent purpose that the shop supports, its current state, a description, and links to the shop’s policies.

Shopify storefronts advertise at least these consent purposes:

  • dev.ucp.consent.analytics
  • dev.ucp.consent.preferences
  • dev.ucp.consent.sale_or_sharing
  • dev.ucp.consent.marketing, with email and sms segments

You can send the buyer’s consent choices when you create, update, or complete a cart or checkout. If you don’t send consent, Shopify applies the shop’s default settings for the buyer’s country. If the buyer's country is unkown, consent defaults to opt-out.

Some choices require a contact detail, such as an SMS opt-in without a phone number. In that case, the response includes a missing_consent_data warning, and the checkout can’t complete until you provide the missing detail.

Who's affected

Platforms and agents that use Checkout MCP or Cart MCP with UCP 2026-08-25 and negotiate the dev.ucp.shopping.buyer_consent extension are affected.

Integrations that don’t declare this extension, or that negotiate an earlier UCP version, aren’t affected.

Why this matters

This change lets your agent present accurate, store-specific consent options during cart and checkout, record the buyer’s explicit choices, and respect the shop’s default rules when consent isn’t provided. This reduces custom logic for regional defaults and helps merchants meet their consent and communication requirements.

What to do

  1. Declare the dev.ucp.shopping.buyer_consent extension at version 2026-08-25 in your agent profile.
  2. When you render cart or checkout, show each consent option to the buyer using the shop’s description and policy links from buyer.consent.
  3. When the buyer makes a choice, send that choice back on cart and checkout create, update, or complete calls, and set source: "platform" only for choices that the buyer actually made during your flow.
  4. If you receive a missing_consent_data warning, collect the required contact detail from the buyer and retry so the checkout can complete.

Related docs

  • Understand Carts and Checkout MCP for agents
  • Configure agent profiles and UCP negotiation
  • Review the UCP buyer consent specification

title: Build with confidence: Shopify AI Toolkit's security check
summary:
Every app install is an act of trust. Merchants rely on your apps to run their business and trust them to protect their orders, customers, and revenue. Protecting merchants is work we share.

AI is helping developers build apps and ship faster. But those same capabilities also help attackers find and exploit security gaps with less time, effort, and cost.

As the way we build evolves, so do our defenses. We continually invest in platform protections, developer tools, and guidance to make secure development easier.

Today, we’re adding another tool to support that work.

Check for vulnerabilities: a security tool built for Shopify apps

Introducing shopify app security check, a new command in Shopify’s AI Toolkit and CLI that finds security vulnerabilities in your app before attackers do.

Run it before you submit an app and on every new release to find potential vulnerabilities in your own code. The check is built around the most common vulnerability patterns in Shopify apps and looks at everything from your app’s codebase, its configurations across every extension point, and the dependencies it relies on.

Each finding shows where the problem is, why it matters, and how to fix it, so you can hand it straight to your agent to review and work through. It runs locally on your development machine.

We've been testing it with a small group of partners who reported finding vulnerabilities they weren’t aware of, including gaps in authentication and in how merchant data was isolated across stores, and were able to level up their security posture by running the command and iterating with their agent.

Now it’s your turn.

Run it

With Shopify AI Toolkit installed, ask your coding agent: /shopify Check my app for common security vulnerabilities

This directs your agent to run shopify app security check using Shopify CLI. Run it directly to see the provided prompts and context.

And because your agent reads your code, the check isn’t tied to one framework. It supports both public and custom apps, whether you use React Router, Rails, Django, Laravel, or custom authentication, it examines how your app actually works and knows what gaps to look for.

Fix what it finds

Each finding includes:

  • The affected file and line
  • The severity and why the issue matters
  • A code example showing how to fix it and deep links to our documentation

Start with critical and high-severity findings. Work through them with your coding agent or fix them yourself, review the changes, and run the check again.

Make it part of every release. A clean report isn’t a guarantee of security: use it alongside your existing tools and reviews.

Help make the tool better

Security is a shared responsibility. We made the tool open source so Shopify and app developers can improve it together.

Share your feedback with us in the Forum, or contribute improvements directly through the open-source GitHub repository. Your feedback helps make future checks more useful for everyone.

Securing the ecosystem is a priority and one we will continue to invest in, including existing measures you can find here. If you haven't adopted these, now's the time.

Run the check on your app today, then fix what it finds to keep your app secured. Apps that keep up with security guidelines will be in the best position to protect merchants and their business. It’s essential that we prioritize this work together.

title: Hydrogen 2026-10 is now available
summary:
The new Hydrogen is generally available today. Since the developer preview started in June, we've shipped seven releases based on feedback from developers using it.

The big deal about the new Hydrogen is that it isn't a big deal: Hydrogen now works with any JavaScript framework. You can bring Shopify's commerce to your stack just by adding the library to your app, instead of needing to replatform.

Hydrogen then handles commerce for you: the cart, variant selection, prices in the buyer's currency, analytics that respect consent, Shop Pay, and customer login. React Router and Next.js have starters ready to deploy, and you can host it anywhere, including Oxygen, which is still free.

The package also includes skills that teach coding agents how to use it. To try it in an existing project, run npx @shopify/hydrogen@latest setup and ask your agent to "Set up my store with Shopify."

What Hydrogen gives you

Every Shopify storefront needs the same commerce pieces, and they're harder to get right than they look. The cart has to stay correct when a shopper taps "Add to cart" twice. Prices have to match the buyer's country and currency. Analytics have to respect consent and still reach Shopify, or your reports go quiet.

Hydrogen handles those for you: the cart, product variants, collection filters, predictive search, Markets, analytics, Shop Pay, and customer accounts. Your framework keeps routing, data loading, and rendering, and the design is all yours.

The glue code fits in a few lines. For instance, a dynamically updating cart count in React looks like this:

import { createCartComponents } from "@shopify/hydrogen/react";

const { CartProvider, useCart } = createCartComponents();

function CartCount() {
  const count = useCart((cart) => cart.data.totalQuantity);
  return {count};
}

Vue has the same thing as a composable, and other frameworks subscribe to the cart directly.

Built for coding agents

Hydrogen comes with 20 skills that teach coding agents how to use it, covering each part of a storefront. We wrote them by building storefronts with agents and fixing the skill every time an agent got something wrong. Ask your agent to "Set up my store with Shopify," and it builds the home, collection, search, product, cart, and account pages, adds analytics, and smoke-tests the result.

The skills live in your project and match the version of Hydrogen you installed, so your agent follows instructions for the code you actually have. After you upgrade Hydrogen versions, you can update the skills with npx @shopify/hydrogen skills sync.

Hydrogen storefronts also work with shopping agents. In browsers that support WebMCP, an agent can search your catalog and update the cart, and after the buyer confirms, Shopify Checkout can submit the order with complete_checkout. You don't have to build anything for it.

Hydrogen uses the same standard storefront actions as Liquid themes, so compatible apps, storefront UI, and agents can share the same cart contract. An app or agent adds to the cart by calling the same action your own UI uses:

await window.Shopify.actions.updateCart({
  lines: [{ merchandiseId: "gid://shopify/ProductVariant/123", quantity: 1 }],
});

If you've used Hydrogen before

Hydrogen used to be a framework built on React Router. To use its cart or analytics, you built your whole storefront on it. Now it's a library, so you can add it to the framework you already use and host it wherever you want. Oxygen is still free.

Existing Hydrogen storefronts keep working as they do now, and there's nothing you need to do today. When you're ready to move, the migration skill walks your agent through it. You keep your pages and routes and swap where the commerce code comes from.

Get started

There are a few ways to get started:

  • Run npx @shopify/hydrogen@latest setup in your own project.
  • Deploy the React Router template to Oxygen from your Shopify admin.
  • If you use Next.js, clone Vercel Shop, a storefront built on Hydrogen and maintained by Vercel.

If something's missing or broken, tell us in the Shopify developer community. The code is on GitHub, and the docs are on shopify.dev.
